notes.audience: Developers and self-hosters running local LLMs on Linux VPS or GPU servers looking to maximize model accuracy and reduce RAM/VRAM footprint.
notes.angle: LookAtMyQuant acts as an intelligent quantization compiler that compresses LLMs to the exact same size as llama.cpp's Q4_K_M but with up to 12× lower KL divergence and significantly higher reasoning accuracy.

facts.fact: LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler and runtime that measures output damage per piece before picking compression codes.
facts.quote: The compiler measures how much compressing each stored piece of a model hurts its output, then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.

facts.fact: On Gemma 4 E2B, LookAtMyQuant's compiled file achieves 12 times lower KL divergence compared to llama.cpp Q4_K_M at equivalent file size.
facts.quote: At the size of llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, the compiled file has 12 times lower KL divergence from the original model, and it solves 59% of GSM8K problems against 50% for Q4_K_M and 61% for the original.

facts.fact: Gemma 4 E2B's per-layer lookup table contains 2.35 billion of its 4.63 billion text weights.
facts.quote: Together these vectors form a table of 262,144 rows by 8,960 columns, which holds 2.35 billion of the model's 4.63 billion text weights.

facts.fact: While llama.cpp stores Gemma's lookup table at Q6_K taking 1.93 GB, LookAtMyQuant drops it to IQ4_XS (4.25 bits) to save 0.68 GB for the actual matrices.
facts.quote: llama.cpp's Q4_K_M recipe stores this table at Q6_K, 6.56 bits per weight. That is 1.93 GB, 56% of the file. The compiler, choosing among the same llama.cpp types, stores it at IQ4_XS, 4.25 bits

facts.fact: LookAtMyQuant allocates saved bit budget to weight matrices, storing most at Q8_0 or BF16.
facts.quote: and gives the 0.68 GB it saves to the matrices, most of which it stores at Q8_0 or BF16

facts.fact: LookAtMyQuant's custom trellis and Lloyd-Max codes beat all public files under 3.5 GB using only 2.0 GB while achieving 60.4% on GSM8K.
facts.quote: With both kinds of code, its 2.00 GB plan has a KL of 0.074, lower than every public file under 3.5 GB, and solves 60.4% of GSM8K problems.

facts.fact: Qwen3.8-27B is compressed from 53.7 GB down to 7.2 GB at 2.1 bits per weight.
facts.quote: The LookAtMyQuant 2 recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB (2.1 bits per weight), calibrated and distilled on English prose, chat, code, and math.

facts.fact: In linear-attention input matrices, 10% of rows carry 79% of the Fisher information, justifying non-uniform per-row bit allocation.
facts.quote: In the matrices that read a linear-attention layer's input, 10% of the rows carry 79% of the total.

facts.fact: LookAtMyQuant's distills models over 4,000 steps with an unusual mid-training re-quantization from the original weights.
facts.quote: So between steps 1,000 and 1,750, each layer is re-quantized once from the original weights W0 in place of W.

# LookAtMyQuant

LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler and runtime. The compiler measures how much compressing each stored piece of a model hurts its output, then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.

The papers, methods, and full results are at [lookatmyquant.com](https://lookatmyquant.com/) ([compiler paper](https://lookatmyquant.com/compiler/), [LookAtMyQuant 2](https://lookatmyquant.com/2/)), and all published checkpoints are on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/shinmegamiboson). The code is under the MIT license.

## Published models

### Inkling-2-Mini (3.9 GB to 12.8 GB)

Six Apple Silicon MLX and NVIDIA CUDA builds of [`thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini`](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini) (26.4B parameters, 5.4B active, 18.89 GB of native text weights) spanning 8 GB devices up to teacher parity. They combine 4 KB SRAM hashed block-vector trellis codes, row trellis codes, per-row-group Fisher outlier allocation, exact native `NVFP4` passthrough on the highest-sensitivity expert buckets at 8.9–12.8 GB, and chat-templated proximal polish (v5).

All six builds were evaluated directly on the shipped packed artifacts against the BF16 teacher (`max_new_tokens = 1,536`, greedy, `reasoning_effort="none"`) on `openai/gsm8k` (`test[:200]`), all 164 `openai/openai_humaneval` problems (strict `<|content_text|>` execution), and 13-language / 6-class chat-templated KL windows. At low bit rates, most remaining HumanEval misses happen when long `<|content_thinking|>` traces exhaust the 1,536-token limit before answering; passing `--max-thinking-tokens 960` closes thinking cleanly at a sentence or newline boundary so the model finishes its answer. Below, unmodified → cap 960 shows scores without and with that cap:

### Qwen3.8-27B in 7.2 GB

The LookAtMyQuant 2 recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB (2.1 bits per weight), calibrated and distilled on English prose, chat, code, and math. [The packed file](https://huggingface.co/shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB) solves 401 of 540 exact-answer math problems — matching the original — while Unsloth's same-size `UD-IQ2_XXS` GGUF solves 348. It also scores above that GGUF on HumanEval (73.8% vs. 67.1%), MMLU (78.8% vs. 75.0%), and GSM8K (94.5% vs. 92.7%).

### LookAtMyQuant 2: Qwen3.5-4B in 1.2 GB

[LookAtMyQuant 2](https://lookatmyquant.com/2/) compresses Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB (2.3 bits per weight). It solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems — against 328 for Prism ML's 1.20 GB Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B and 359 for the original — and lowers held-out text KL from 0.59 to 0.45 nats.

The recipe is trellis post-training quantization calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions (with digit tokens weighted 10× and bits allocated per row by Fisher information), followed by 4,000 steps of distillation in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights (5.4 GPU-hours; see [LookAtMyQuant 2 recipe on Qwen3.5-4B](#lookatmyquant-2-recipe-on-qwen35-4b)).

The 1.23 GB file is on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.5-4B-LookAtMyQuant-1.2GB) and in the [`lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb` release](https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant/releases/tag/lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb). Its 464 MB 4-bit DSpine drafter ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.5-4B-LookAtMyQuant-1.2GB-drafter) / [`lm2-drafter-4bit` release](https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant/releases/tag/lm2-drafter-4bit)) runs 1.5–2.0× faster on Apple silicon with identical greedy output (176 vs. 88 tok/s on an M5 Max across 30 held-out prompts).

## Quick start

### Apple Silicon (MLX)

Install the runtime package directly (installs `mlx`, `mlx-lm`, `numpy`, and `huggingface-hub` without the PyTorch compiler dependencies):

```sh
pip install git+https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant.git
```

From a local clone, `pip install -e .` installs the `lamq` command, or run `python -m runtime_mlx` without installing.

**CLI.** Pass a local model folder or a Hugging Face repo ID:

```sh
lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter \
    --max-thinking-tokens 960 \
    -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." --stats

lamq chat shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    -p "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals." --stats

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.5-4B-LookAtMyQuant-1.2GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.5-4B-LookAtMyQuant-1.2GB-drafter \
    -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." --stats
```

`lamq generate` reads stdin when `-p` is omitted and supports `--raw`, `--system`, `--thinking`, `--max-thinking-tokens`, `--temp`, `--top-p`, `--mode linear|chat-fork|copy-wide`, `--no-adaptive`, `--prefill-chunk N` (`-1` auto, `0` single pass), and `--json`. `lamq info ` inspects a packed model's format and dimensions without loading weights.

Inkling prefill runs in one pass when the prompt fits the estimated MLX memory budget and chunks automatically under pressure. To shrink global attention cache memory on long prompts, set `LAMQ_GLOBAL_KV=fp8` or `LAMQ_GLOBAL_KV=q4` (default `fp16`; sliding-window attention stays FP16; either option can change generated tokens).

**Python API.** `runtime_mlx.load` returns a `(model, tokenizer)` pair compatible with `mlx_lm.generate` and `mlx_lm.stream_generate` (auto-detecting `opgraph-packed-1`, `inkling2-packed`, and `lamq.json` exports):

```python
from mlx_lm import generate
from runtime_mlx import load

model, tok = load("shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB")
prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps."}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False,
)
print(generate(model, tok, prompt, max_tokens=200))
```

For streaming, multi-turn chat, or speculative decoding through one interface, use `Runtime`:

```python
from runtime_mlx import Runtime

rt = Runtime.load(
    "shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB",
    drafter="shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter",
)
for chunk in rt.stream(
    "Solve 3x + 4y = 31 and 5x - 2y = 17.",
    max_tokens=1536,
    max_thinking_tokens=960,
):
    print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)
```

### NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA)

Install the CUDA extra on a machine with a supported NVIDIA GPU. The model IDs and chat templates are shared with the Apple Silicon runtime:

```sh
pip install -e ".[cuda]"
lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-8.9GB --device cuda -p "What is 17 times 23?"
lamq serve shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-8.9GB --device cuda
```

Triton handles ordinary generation and `NVFP4` experts; the native CUDA engine adds DSpark speculative decoding on trellis packs. Set `LAMQ_CUDA_GLOBAL_KV=q8_0` or `q4_0` to compress global KV caches, and `LAMQ_CUDA_KV_VRAM_CELLS` to spill older cache cells to pinned host memory. See [`runtime_cuda/README.md`](runtime_cuda/README.md) for model support, short size aliases, revision selection, and tuning commands.

### HTTP server and browser chat (`lamq serve`)

`lamq serve` serves a packed Inkling-2-Mini model over HTTP on Apple Silicon or CUDA (`--device cuda`):

```sh
lamq serve shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter --port 8080 --ui

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 23?"}], "reasoning_effort": "low"}'
```

- **Endpoints:** OpenAI `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses` (Codex CLI), Anthropic `/v1/messages` (Claude Code; `developer` messages map to `system`), `/v1/models`, `/health`, plus `POST /apply-template` and `POST /tokenize`. Supports streaming, `reasoning_effort` (`reasoning_content`), and `tools` (`"tool_choice": "auto"` or `"none"`; forced tool calls return HTTP 400).
- **Browser chat (`--ui`):** Serves a streaming chat UI at `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` that keeps the conversation and draft in session storage, with settings for reasoning and output length and expandable timing/token usage. Browser-origin API calls are disabled by default; for remote access behind an HTTPS proxy, preserve the browser's `Host` header (including any non-default port) and disable response buffering. The page itself is public and prompts for the API key when auth is enabled.
- **Batching and prompt caching:** On Apple Silicon MLX, `lamq serve` runs continuous batching by default (`--max-batch 32`) with paged KV pools, automatic zero-copy shared-prefix reuse on loopback (`--no-prefix-cache` disables it), interleaved chunked prefill (`--prefill-step 512`), and load-adaptive DSpark (`--dspark-max-batch 4`). Pass `--max-batch 1` for single-stream serving, where `--prompt-cache N` keeps up to `N` in-memory KV snapshots and `--prompt-cache-dir PATH` persists incremental deltas to disk across restarts (capped by `--prompt-cache-gb`, default `20`; passing `--prompt-cache-dir` selects single-stream mode automatically). ABSTRACT

Most quantized language models use one format and one bit width for every tensor, with a few hand-written exceptions. LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the whole model when that piece alone is compressed. The pieces are every weight matrix, buckets of embedding rows grouped by token frequency, and each layer's key–value cache. It measures a few codes for each piece and predicts the rest. Then it gives each piece the code that keeps total damage lowest while the model fits the size or speed budget of a target device.

Each code is a short program in a grammar of tensor-network rewrites. Nine published quantization and pruning methods are short programs in this grammar, reproduced exactly.

On Gemma 4 E2B, the compiler restricted to llama.cpp's types makes ordinary GGUF files. At the size of llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, the compiled file has 12 times lower KL divergence from the original model, and it solves 59% of GSM8K problems against 50% for Q4_K_M and 61% for the original. Most of the gain comes from Gemma's 2.35-billion-weight per-layer lookup table. It is cheap to compress, so the compiler stores it at 4.25 bits instead of 6.56 and gives the saved bytes to the matrices. On Qwen3.5-4B and SmolLM2-360M, compared with 3-bit models that keep the embedding or the cache at 16 bits, the compiler's plans have 6 to 81 times lower KL at equal cost on each target device.

Every piece of a model costs something different to compress

A quantization format applies one rule to a whole model. GGUF's Q4_K_M, for example, stores most matrices at about 4.5 bits per weight and a fixed list of tensors at Q6_K. The rule is the same for a 360-million-parameter model and a 70-billion-parameter one, for a model with a large vocabulary and one with a small one, and for a phone and a server.

But the damage each piece does to the model is not uniform. In Gemma 4 E2B, one 0.4-million-weight matrix costs nearly as much at 3 bits as twenty whole layers. Half of the model's weights are a lookup table that tolerates 4 bits well. The 256 most frequent tokens make up a third of all text, while the rarest half of the vocabulary makes up a fraction of a percent. A fixed recipe ignores these differences.

LookAtMyQuant makes a plan that names one code for every stored piece of the model. It finds the plan that does the least damage within a given budget on a given device. We make four contributions:

A quantization compiler. It allocates bits across weight matrices, frequency buckets of the embedding and per-layer tables, and the key–value cache, with costs that depend on the target device.
A cheap way to measure. One forward pass with shaped noise predicts each matrix's damage at 3 bits, and the ratios between codes are the same on every model we tested. Measuring a few layers with real codes is then enough to predict every other code.
Compiled GGUF files for Gemma 4 E2B that beat every public quantization we measured, scored the same way, at every size where a public file exists.
A grammar of quantization programs in which published methods are short programs, so one plan can mix different kinds of code.
A compiled Gemma 4 E2B file has 12 times lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same size

We compared the compiler's files with every widely used quantization of Gemma 4 E2B that we could load. These are Google's quantization-aware-trained q4_0 GGUF, unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL, bartowski's Q4_K_M and LM Studio's MLX 4-bit. We also built llama.cpp's stock recipes, Q2_K to Q8_0, with an importance matrix from the same calibration text the compiler uses.

Every file is turned back into full-precision weights inside the same Hugging Face model, so the same code scores every file on the same text. The text is 64 windows of WikiText-2 and 8 held-out windows from each of 13 sources: English, ten other languages, code and chat. Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B [1] is Prism ML's ternary-weight version of Qwen3.5-4B [2]. It stores 2-bit codes with a scale and a bias per 128 weights, and its language-model weights take 1.20 GB. The original's take 8.4 GB in bf16.

Our file is the same model at 2.3 bits per weight, 1.23 GB. It is post-training quantization with trellis codes from the LookAtMyQuant compiler, followed by 4,000 steps of distillation from the original. The packed file is published on Hugging Face (and mirrored as a GitHub release).

The math test is 540 generated problems with exact integer or fraction answers, in twelve families at three difficulties, from long addition to determinants and modular exponentiation. Scoring is exact match on the final boxed answer. Decoding is greedy with thinking disabled and at most 2,048 new tokens.

Ours solves 330, Bonsai 328 and the original 359. 62 problems are solved only by ours and 60 only by Bonsai (McNemar p = 0.93), so the test does not separate the two files.

On text, ours is closer to the original. KL(original ‖ model) on held-out text from 13 sources is 0.45 nats for ours and 0.59 for Bonsai, and ours is lower on 11 of the 13 (Figure 2). Bonsai is lower on chat and Hindi.

All sizes are the language model alone. Qwen3.5-4B also has a 0.67 GB vision tower, which Bonsai's 1.87 GB download keeps in bf16. Our file omits it, and we did not evaluate image inputs.

A 4B model at 2.3 bits beats a 2B at 5 bits and a 0.8B at 8 bits

The same space can hold a smaller model at a higher bit rate. We quantized the two smaller Qwen3.5 models the way MLX's standard files do [8]: affine quantization in groups of 64 weights, each with a 16-bit scale and bias, which costs N + 0.5 bits per weight at N bits.

Qwen3.5-2B at 5 bits is 1.29 GB and solves 284. At 4 bits it is 1.06 GB and solves 242. Qwen3.5-0.8B at 8 bits is 0.80 GB and solves 205; more bits would not help it, since its relative weight error at 8 bits is already 0.5%. Their KL from the original 4B on text is 0.51, 0.60 and 0.75, against 0.45 for ours.

At 2.3 bits, two files with nearly equal KL solve 1 and 328 problems

A scalar Lloyd–Max build at this size, calibrated on generic text, has WikiText-2 KL 0.60. Bonsai's is 0.50. The build solves 1 problem of 540 and Bonsai solves 328. That likelihood metrics miss reasoning at low bit rates is known. ThinkBit [16] and LAQuant [17] report it for perplexity at 2 and 3 bits. This pair shows the same for KL from the original.

The two metrics also separate in the other direction. Our post-training build already solves 317 at a KL of 1.41 on the 13 sources. Fine-tuning then cuts that KL to 0.45 and adds 13 problems. Calibrating on the model's own long worked solutions, with digit tokens weighted 10×, nearly doubled the score at fixed codes

Layer-wise quantization minimizes error under the input second moment H = E[w·xxᵀ], so the calibration set and the token weights w decide which errors count. Weighting tokens in H is RSQ's method [12], which weights by attention score. Calibrating on the model's own reasoning traces is AYOT's [13]. Here the weight follows the kind of token a position predicts, chosen for the capability to keep.

With trellis codes fixed and half of the set the original's GSM8K solutions [10], the build solves 117.

An all-math set with w = 1 at positions that predict a digit and w = 0.1 elsewhere gives 147. Replacing 256 sequences of 512 tokens with 64 of 2,048, the original's greedy solutions to MATH training problems [9], gives 224. These have long chains of intermediate results, like the benchmark's.

Bits belong to rows: 10% of a matrix's rows can carry 79% of its Fisher information

For each output row i we measure si = E[gi²]·E[yi²] on the original model. Here y is the row's output and g is the gradient of the log-likelihood of tokens sampled from the model's own predictions, taken at the positions the calibration weights most, those that predict a digit. In the matrices that read a linear-attention layer's input, 10% of the rows carry 79% of the total.

Mixed precision between output rows, ranked across the whole model, is MixLLM's [14]. RoleQ [15] gives a second ternary plane to units chosen by Fisher saliency. We apply the idea to trellis codes, at four rates inside a matrix.

A global allocation of 1 to 4 bits per row group, across all matrices and under the same byte budget, took the score from 265 to 300. It puts 13% of the matrix weights at 1 bit, 47% at 2, 36% at 3 and 4% at 4. Rotating the output side as well would average this structure away, so the incoherence transform is on the input side only.

e-means codebooks cut trellis MSE by 4% to 9% at the same bytes and added 17 problems

A trellis code decodes each weight from a 4,096-entry codebook. We had fit it with six full-batch Lloyd iterations on a fixed set of Gaussian sequences. e-means [7] replaces full passes with mini-batch updates through exponential moving averages. Fit that way, with fresh Gaussian samples in every batch, an EMA of the sum and count for each codeword, and a batch weight on a cosine schedule from 0.5 to 0.01, the codebook's MSE under the deployed encoder falls 4.0%, 4.5%, 6.2% and 8.8% at 1 to 4 bits.

The file size and the decoder do not change. The score went from 300 to 317, and KL on the 13 sources fell 4%. With e-means codebooks at 2 and 3 bits only, the score was 311.

Error propagation at half strength beat full strength by 41 problems

QEP [6] adds a cross term to the layer objective, so that the quantized layer on quantized inputs matches the original layer on clean inputs, with a strength α. At α = 1 the build solves 224. At α = 0.5 it solves 265, and WikiText-2 KL falls from 0.85 to 0.66.

Re-quantizing every layer from the original weights mid-training cut KL on text by another 43%

Our fine-tuning is distillation on latent full-precision weights W that are pulled toward their quantized values P and re-quantized every 1,000 steps (Figure 5). Its parts are published. TVQ [18] trains trellis codes through latent weights and recomputes their indices every 16 steps, with a straight-through estimator. The pull is ProxQuant's and BinaryRelax's [20] [21]. It took the score from 317 to 321 and KL on the 13 sources from 1.41 to 0.79. The codes hardly moved: 0.1% of a layer's codes change at a re-quantization, because a weight held near its quantized value quantizes back to the same code. BCJR-QAT [19] describes the same effect: trained latent weights stay in the basin of the post-training solution.

So between steps 1,000 and 1,750, each layer is re-quantized once from the original weights W0 in place of W. H comes from an exponential moving average over the training batches' own activations, about 2,000 sequences of the partly fine-tuned model, eight times the build's calibration tokens. 97% of the codes change, W restarts at the new P, and training continues. We know of no earlier method that returns to the original weights during training.

On two builds this gave 330 and 324 problems at KL 0.45 and 0.45, against 321 and 314 at 0.79 and 0.80 without it (Table 2). Part of the gain on text comes from the data mix: the running H is 30% non-math text, and the build's calibration set is all math.
